text_blocks.snippet: Neither SGLT2 inhibitors nor GLP-1 receptor agonists are universally prescribed as standalone first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes; remains the classic foundational first-line medication, though current guidelines from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommend adding SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists early—often alongside metformin—based on individual patient comorbidities.

text_blocks.snippet: Key Comparisons: SGLT2 Inhibitors vs. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

table: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (e.g., dulaglutide, semaglutide, liraglutide)
Subcutaneous injection (daily/weekly) or oral semaglutide (daily pill)
Blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidneys, causing excess sugar to pass in the urine ( glucosuria)
Stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release, slows gastric emptying, and suppresses appetite
Superior benefit in reducing heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular outcomes
Reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), cardiovascular death, stroke, and heart attack
Outperforms GLP-1 RAs for slowing chronic kidney disease progression and acute kidney injury
Provides moderate renal protection (largely driven by reducing albuminuria)

list.snippet: Choose an SGLT2 Inhibitor First (or alongside metformin) if:
The patient has a history of heart failure (HF) or a high risk of heart failure.
The patient has chronic kidney disease (CKD) or reduced eGFR, where SGLT2 inhibitors offer superior kidney protection.
An oral, once-daily pill is strongly preferred over an injectable medication.
Choose a GLP-1 Receptor Agonist First (or alongside metformin) if:
The patient needs stronger A1C lowering or more aggressive weight loss management (such as co-existing severe obesity).
The patient has atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or a high risk of stroke/heart attack.
In many high-risk patients, both classes are used together (or added to metformin) because their organ-protecting and metabolic profiles are complementary rather than interchangeable.
